templates.name: Nutrient management
templates.subject: How can macroalgae help manage nitrate?
templates.preview: A closer look at nutrient uptake, healthy growth, and regular harvesting.
templates.heading: How can macroalgae help manage nitrate?
templates.body: Macroalgae use nutrients from aquarium water to build new growth. That growth can help manage nitrate, provided the algae have suitable conditions and are harvested regularly. Here’s how the process fits into aquarium care.

fields.label: A close look at the tangled green growth of Chaetomorpha destination
A close look at the tangled green growth of Chaetomorpha

text.text-2: Chaeto grows as a loose tangle of green strands, rather than attaching to rock or substrate. This makes it easy to divide as it expands. Harvesting a portion carries nutrients stored in that growth out of the aquarium.
text.text-3: Provide suitable light and steady water movement, and leave space for new growth between harvests.
text.text-5: What to watch as it grows
text.text-6: Look for ongoing growth and follow nitrate and phosphate readings over time. If growth slows, check lighting, water movement, and available space before adding more algae. Continue regular aquarium maintenance as you assess the trend.
text.text-9: covers care requirements and compatibility to help you choose macroalgae suited to your setup.

templates.name: Habitat article
templates.subject: What lives among your macroalgae?
templates.preview: A closer look at the small animals that use macroalgae as habitat.
templates.heading: What lives among your macroalgae?
templates.body: A clump of macroalgae is also a place for small animals to live. Its fronds and branches provide cover for tiny crustaceans that are easy to miss during a quick look at the tank.

fields.label: Pom Pom macroalgae showing its fine, densely branching red fronds
Codium macroalgae showing its thick green branches

text.text-0: Pom Pom’s fine fronds and Codium’s thicker branches illustrate the varied structures macroalgae add to a planted aquarium.
text.text-1: Copepods and amphipods can live among macroalgae, with some becoming food for fish and other reef animals. In a refugium, reduced access from fish can give these populations more opportunity to grow.
text.text-2: The shelter still depends on the animals sharing that space. Mysids, for example, are vulnerable to fish that hunt small crustaceans; hiding places and low predation pressure help them establish.
text.text-3: A closer look when you harvest
text.text-4: When you harvest, gently shake the removed clump in aquarium water before discarding it. This can release some of its small inhabitants back into the refugium.
text.text-5: Our species library explores the habitat, behavior, and care of macroalgae and marine invertebrates.

templates.name: Species field guide
templates.subject: How Halimeda helps form reef sand
templates.preview: The biology behind its firm segments, and what it means in an aquarium.
templates.heading: Halimeda, from seaweed to sand
templates.body: Halimeda grows in chains of firm green segments. Calcium carbonate gives those segments their structure, and helps explain how this living seaweed can eventually become part of the sand around a reef.

fields.label: Halimeda macroalgae with branching chains of green, coinlike segments

text.text-9: Halimeda deposits calcium carbonate within its body, forming rigid segments connected by more flexible joints. Although the segments look like small leaves, they are parts of the algal body. This gives Halimeda its distinctive articulated growth.
text.text-11: In natural reef environments, old or detached segments can lose their living tissue and break into smaller carbonate fragments. Over time, those fragments can become part of the sediment around a reef, alongside material from other organisms with carbonate structures.
text.text-14: For aquarium keepers, that mineral structure has a practical implication: growing Halimeda uses calcium and alkalinity. Include both in routine testing, and maintain stable conditions alongside suitable lighting and water movement. Its firm, branching growth adds a different texture to a planted display.

image-1.alt: Halimeda macroalgae with branching chains of green, coinlike segments
